title: Homecoming and Semester
premise: Ada Pemberton has spent four years at Hollow Creek High perfecting invisibility, until her history teacher pairs her with Cole Brantley — golden boy, son of the family that owns half the town — for a semester project documenting the town's founding tradition: the Harvest Home festival. Digging into archives, Ada discovers the festival's origin story is a sanitized lie that erased the family who actually built it, a Black homesteading family whose descendants include her late grandmother. As Cole's father moves to sell the festival grounds to developers, Ada must choose between staying hidden and claiming a legacy that could cost her Cole's loyalty and the town's goodwill. She ends the semester by telling the true story at Harvest Home itself, winning the fight to save the grounds and discovering that love — for a person, a place, and a truth — is worth standing in the open.
about_author: August Delacroix grew up in a small farming town where everyone knew everyone's business except their own, an experience that fuels his stories about teenagers outgrowing the silences their towns are built on. He writes from a converted grain barn, where he keeps his grandmother's county fair ribbons pinned above the desk.

chapters.title: The Invisible Girl's Map
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Opening day of senior year; Ada narrates her survival strategy of small-town anonymity through her mental map of safe routes, safe seats, safe silences. When Mr. Okafor announces semester-long paired projects, dread spikes as he reads 'Pemberton and Brantley.' Emotional beat: the cost of hiding, and the first crack in it.

chapters.title: Assigned Enemies
chapters.summary: Alternating Ada and Cole POV. First library meeting goes badly — Cole assumes she'll do the work, Ada calls him a mascot for his family's name. They grudgingly split the Harvest Home research: he takes oral histories, she takes archives. Emotional beat: mutual contempt masking mutual curiosity.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Says
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. In the county archive, Ada finds an 1898 land ledger naming the Trueblood family — including her great-great-grandmother Ruth — as original donors of the festival grounds, a name absent from every plaque. She says nothing to Cole yet. Emotional beat: the thrill and terror of inheritance discovered in silence.

chapters.title: Oral History, Oral Wounds
chapters.summary: Cole's POV. Interviewing his grandfather for the project, Cole hears the official founding story delivered with a strange flatness, and catches his grandfather changing the subject when Ada's surname comes up. Meanwhile he notices Ada watching him like she's waiting for him to fail her. Emotional beat: first doubt in the story he was raised on.

chapters.title: Detention and Confession
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Paired detention (a prank neither admits to) forces real conversation; Ada tests Cole with a half-truth about the ledger, and he doesn't flinch — instead he shows her a developer's survey map he found in his father's truck. The grounds are already spoken for. Emotional beat: alliance formed over shared alarm.

chapters.title: Ruth Trueblood's Field
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada walks the overgrown edge of the festival grounds with her mother, who finally tells the family version: how Ruth donated the land for a harvest gathering meant for everyone, and how the town thanked her by forgetting her. Ada decides the project will tell the whole story. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: The Draft That Starts a Fire
chapters.summary: Cole's POV. Cole submits their draft naming the Truebloods; his father reads it over his shoulder and orders it cut, revealing he's known the erasure was deliberate and profitable. Cole refuses, and his father threatens both the sale timeline and Cole's college fund. Emotional beat: loyalty to family cracking against loyalty to truth.

chapters.title: Locker Shut, Door Open
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Someone scrawls 'know your place' inside Ada's locker after word spreads about the draft; Cole publicly defends her in the hallway, costing him his friend group. Ada, humiliated and furious, nearly quits — then finds Ruth's name carved inside the old festival stage beam. Emotional beat: lowest point, and the reason to keep going.

chapters.title: Harvest Home Eve
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The night before the festival, Ada and Cole race to present their findings to the town council before the sale vote; Mr. Okafor stakes his job on letting the students speak. Cole's grandfather, confronted with the ledger, quietly confirms everything — and hands Cole Ruth's original deed copy. Emotional beat: fear sharpened into resolve on the eve of judgment.

chapters.title: Homecoming
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. At Harvest Home, Ada tells Ruth's story from the old stage to nine hundred neighbors, voice shaking and unhidden; the council tables the sale pending landmark review, and the crowd — slowly, imperfectly — applauds. Cole stands beside her, hand in hers, in front of everyone. Emotional beat: love against duty resolved into love as duty kept; Ada finally visible, and home.
